name: OSII NASA facts pilot v1
description: Small manually curated NASA-derived fact summaries, checked November 10, 2026. A reproducible integration pilot, not a representative RAG benchmark. Source text is paraphrased; original documents are linked for verification.

documents.name: mercury.txt
documents.text: Mercury orbit and rotation. Mercury travels around the Sun in 88 Earth days. One rotation of Mercury takes about 59 Earth days. A complete solar day on Mercury lasts 176 Earth days. Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, but Venus is hotter because Venus has a dense atmosphere. Mercury has no moons and no rings.

documents.name: venus.txt
documents.text: Venus orbit and rotation. A sidereal rotation of Venus takes 243 Earth days, longer than its orbital year of 225 Earth days. Venus spins backward compared with Earth; the Sun would rise in the west. Sunrise to sunset takes 117 Earth days. Venus has an axial tilt of only three degrees, too small for noticeable seasons.

documents.name: mars.txt
documents.text: Mars orbit and rotation. A Martian rotation lasts 24.6 hours. Martian days are called sols. A year on Mars is 669.6 sols, equivalent to 687 Earth days. Mars has an axial tilt of 25 degrees and experiences seasons. Its elliptical orbit makes the seasons unequal in length.

documents.name: jupiter.txt
documents.text: Jupiter atmosphere and rotation. Jupiter spins once in roughly 10 hours. Its fast rotation creates strong jet streams that separate the clouds into bright zones and dark belts. The atmosphere has layers associated with ammonia ice, ammonium hydrosulfide, and possibly water ice and vapor. Jupiter is a gas planet with no solid surface.

documents.name: saturn.txt
documents.text: Saturn structure. Saturn is made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Saturn is the only planet in the solar system whose average density is less than water. Its gas-giant structure has no true solid surface. Strong pressures and temperatures inside the planet would destroy a spacecraft trying to pass through it.

documents.name: uranus.txt
documents.text: Uranus tilt and rotation. Uranus has an axial tilt of 97.77 degrees: its equator is nearly perpendicular to its orbit. The unusual tilt creates extreme seasons, including a dark winter lasting about 21 years in one hemisphere. Uranus rotates in the opposite direction from most planets. Venus is the other planet with this backward rotation.

documents.name: neptune.txt
documents.text: Neptune orbit and discovery. Neptune takes about 165 Earth years, or 60,190 Earth days, to complete an orbit. Its rotation lasts about 16 hours. It is about 30 astronomical units from the Sun. Johann Gottfried Galle found Neptune in 1846 using Urbain Joseph Le Verrier's mathematical predictions. Neptune's long year makes its seasons last more than 40 years.
